name: Radia Perlman
milestone_by_age_26: STP invented in 1985 at age 34; by 26 was working as a protocol designer at BBN but had no independently verifiable personal milestone.
early_history_summary: Perlman grew up in New Jersey with both parents working as engineers. She was introduced to programming at MIT as an undergraduate, worked in the Logo Lab and AI Lab, then left grad school around 1976 to join BBN designing packet radio network protocols before moving to DEC in 1980 where she invented Spanning Tree Protocol.
family_context_summary: Both parents were engineers; father worked on radar and mother was a computer programmer. Grew up in New Jersey.
parent_family_domain_summary: Both parents were engineers, providing early exposure to technical thinking, though Perlman reported feeling intimidated by peers with more technical backgrounds.
evidence_summary: Perlman's parents were both engineers, giving her early exposure to technical fields. She attended MIT as an undergraduate where she worked in the Logo Lab and AI Lab. Her seminal contribution, Spanning Tree Protocol, was developed at DEC in 1985 when she was 34, well beyond the age-26 cutoff. By 26 she was at BBN doing protocol design work, but this was a job rather than a distinctive personal milestone.

name: Paul Baran
milestone_by_age_26: Packet switching concept developed at RAND starting 1959 at age 33; by 26 was a technician and field engineer with no notable personal milestone.
early_history_summary: Born in Grodno, Poland, Baran emigrated to Philadelphia as a child. He earned a BS in electrical engineering from Drexel in 1949, then worked as a technician on UNIVAC and on telemetering systems at Cape Canaveral before joining Hughes Aircraft. His seminal packet switching work began at RAND in 1959.
family_context_summary: Born in Grodno, Poland (now Belarus); family emigrated to Philadelphia in 1928. Not documented in reviewed sources.
evidence_summary: Baran emigrated from Poland to Philadelphia as a toddler. He earned his BS in 1949 and worked on early computers (UNIVAC) and telemetering systems, but his seminal contribution — packet switching — came at RAND starting in 1959 when he was 33. By 26 he was a field engineer with no distinctive personal milestone.

name: Donald Davies
milestone_by_age_26: Packet switching invented in 1965 at age 41; by 26 was a team member on the ACE computer project at NPL under Turing but had no personal milestone.
early_history_summary: Born in Treorchy, Wales, Davies lost his father as an infant and moved to Portsmouth with his mother and twin sister. He earned double first-class honors in physics (1943) and mathematics (1947) from Imperial College London, then joined the National Physical Laboratory to work on the ACE computer under Alan Turing. His packet switching work came in 1965.
family_context_summary: Son of a colliery pay clerk who died when Davies was one year old; raised by his mother in Portsmouth after his father's death. Twin sister became a classics scholar.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. Father was a coal mine clerk before his early death.
evidence_summary: Davies overcame early adversity — his father died when he was one — and earned double first-class honors from Imperial College by age 23. He joined Turing's ACE team at NPL in 1947, but his seminal contribution, packet switching, came in 1965 at age 41. By 26 he was a team member on a pioneering computer project, not a personal milestone.

name: Leonard Kleinrock
milestone_by_age_26: Queueing theory thesis completed in 1963 at age 29; by 26 had only a master's degree from MIT and was beginning doctoral work.
early_history_summary: Born in New York City to Austrian Jewish immigrant parents, Kleinrock grew up in the Bronx and attended the Bronx High School of Science. He earned his BEE from CCNY in 1957 (attending night school while working), then went to MIT on a Lincoln Lab Staff Associate fellowship, earning his MS in 1959 and PhD in 1963. His seminal queueing theory work was his doctoral thesis.
family_context_summary: Son of Austrian Jewish immigrants; father wanted him to be an accountant. Grew up in New York City; attended CCNY night school while working at a cousin's electronics firm to support his family.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. Family was working-class; father was not in a technical field.
evidence_summary: Kleinrock grew up in a working-class immigrant family in New York, attending CCNY night school while working. His seminal queueing theory work was his 1963 PhD thesis at MIT, completed at age 29. By 26 he had only a master's degree and was just beginning his doctoral research.

name: J.C.R. Licklider
milestone_by_age_26: Man-Computer Symbiosis paper published in 1960 at age 45; by 26 was a PhD candidate in psychoacoustics at the University of Rochester with no computing milestone.
early_history_summary: Born in St. Louis, Missouri, the son of a Baptist minister, Licklider earned degrees in psychology, mathematics, and physics from Washington University (BA 1937, MA 1938), then a PhD in psychology from the University of Rochester in 1942. He worked at Harvard's Psycho-Acoustic Laboratory during WWII, then joined MIT and later BBN. His influential computing vision came in 1960.
family_context_summary: Born in St. Louis, Missouri; father was a Baptist minister, mother was Margaret Robnett Licklider. Only son in the family.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. Father was a minister, not in a technical or scientific field.
evidence_summary: Licklider was the son of a Baptist minister in St. Louis. He trained in psychology, not computing, earning his PhD in 1942 at age 27. His influential computing work — the Man-Computer Symbiosis paper and ARPA IPTO directorship — came in 1960-1964, well after age 26. By 26 he was still a PhD candidate in psychoacoustics.

name: Douglas Engelbart
milestone_by_age_26: Computer mouse and Mother of All Demos came in the 1960s; by 26 was an electrical engineer at NACA Ames Laboratory with no notable milestone.
early_history_summary: Born in Portland, Oregon, Engelbart grew up on a small farmstead during the Great Depression. His father died when he was nine. He studied electrical engineering at Oregon State, served in the Navy as a radar technician during WWII, then worked at NACA Ames before pursuing graduate work at UC Berkeley (MS 1953, PhD 1955). His seminal work on interactive computing came at SRI in the 1960s.
family_context_summary: Grew up on a small farmstead near Portland, Oregon during the Great Depression. Father was an electrical engineer turned radio shop owner who died when Engelbart was nine. Grandson of early Western pioneers.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father had an electrical engineering background and ran a radio shop in Portland, providing some early exposure to electronics, but died when Engelbart was young.
evidence_summary: Engelbart grew up on a farm during the Depression and lost his father at age nine. He served as a Navy radar technician in WWII, then earned his BS in 1948 and worked at NACA Ames. His vision of interactive computing emerged in 1951, but his seminal contributions — the mouse, hypertext, and the 1968 Mother of All Demos — came in his 30s and 40s. By 26 he was a junior electrical engineer.

name: Alan Kay
milestone_by_age_26: Smalltalk developed at Xerox PARC in the 1970s; by 26 had just completed a bachelor's degree and was starting graduate school at the University of Utah.
early_history_summary: Born in Springfield, Massachusetts, Kay grew up in an environment of art, literature, and science. His father designed prostheses and his mother was a musician. He attended Brooklyn Technical High School, joined the Air Force where he became an IBM 1401 programmer, then earned a BS in mathematics and molecular biology from the University of Colorado in 1966 before starting graduate school at Utah under ARPA funding.
family_context_summary: Father designed arm and leg prostheses; mother was a musician and taught Alan to play music. Grew up in an environment of art, literature, and science; could read by age three and had read about 150 books before starting school.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a prosthetic device designer (engineering/medical domain); mother was a musician. Both contributed to a rich intellectual environment at home.
evidence_summary: Kay grew up in a cultured household with a prosthetic-designer father and musician mother. He learned programming in the Air Force and earned his BS in 1966 at age 26, just starting graduate school. His seminal contributions — Smalltalk, object-oriented programming, the Dynabook concept — came at Xerox PARC in the 1970s when he was in his 30s.

name: Seymour Papert
milestone_by_age_26: Logo programming language created in 1967 at age 39; by 26 held a PhD in mathematics from Witwatersrand but had no distinctive personal milestone in his eventual field.
early_history_summary: Born in Pretoria, South Africa, to a Jewish family, Papert earned a BA in philosophy (1949) and a PhD in mathematics (1952) from the University of the Witwatersrand by age 24. He then went to Cambridge for a second doctorate, worked with Jean Piaget in Geneva, and joined MIT in 1963. His Logo programming language was created in 1967.
family_context_summary: Born to a Jewish family in Pretoria, South Africa. Not documented in reviewed sources beyond this.
evidence_summary: Papert was born in South Africa and earned a PhD in mathematics at 24, which is notable but not a distinctive personal milestone in his eventual field of educational technology and AI. His seminal contributions — Logo, constructionism, and the Perceptrons book with Minsky — came in the 1960s-70s when he was in his late 30s and beyond.

name: Marvin Minsky
milestone_by_age_26: Built SNARC (Stochastic Neural-Analog Reinforcement Calculator) at Princeton in 1951, the first artificial neural network learning machine, while a graduate student.
early_history_summary: Minsky grew up in New York City as the son of an eye surgeon and was encouraged in science from childhood. After Navy service in WWII, he studied mathematics at Harvard (BA 1950) and then pursued a PhD at Princeton, where he built SNARC with fellow student Dean Edmonds, funded by the Office of Naval Research via George Miller.
family_context_summary: Son of Dr. Henry Minsky, chief of ophthalmology at Mount Sinai Hospital, and Fannie Reiser, a social activist and Zionist. Grew up in Manhattan and the Bronx in an upper-middle-class household that actively encouraged scientific curiosity.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a prominent eye surgeon who maintained a science library that Minsky used extensively as a child. Science and medicine were actively encouraged in the household, though the father's domain was medicine rather than computing or AI.
primary_early_advantage_tags: elite schools, Princeton, Harvard, science family, early electronics, Bronx Science
evidence_summary: Minsky was the son of a prominent eye surgeon and grew up in an intellectually rich household with access to his father's science library. He attended elite schools — Fieldston, Bronx High School of Science, and Phillips Academy — before Harvard and Princeton. Inspired by the 1943 McCulloch-Pitts paper on artificial neurons, he built SNARC, the first neural network learning machine, in 1951 at age 24 while a Princeton graduate student, with funding arranged by George Miller and electronics help from Dean Edmonds. John von Neumann and Norbert Wiener were on his thesis committee. The elite institutional pipeline from Bronx Science through Princeton was a dominant early advantage.
starting_point: Born in New York City to Dr. Henry Minsky, chief of ophthalmology at Mount Sinai Hospital, and Fannie Reiser, a social activist and Zionist; grew up in Manhattan and the Bronx in an upper-middle-class household.
current_position: Died January 24, 2016 at age 88 in Boston, Massachusetts; final role: Toshiba Professor of Media Arts and Sciences Emeritus at MIT and co-founder of the MIT AI Laboratory.

trajectory.event: Built SNARC, the first artificial neural network learning machine, while a graduate student at Princeton with funding from the Office of Naval Research.
Completed PhD in mathematics at Princeton with a dissertation on neural-analog reinforcement systems; became a Junior Fellow of the Harvard Society of Fellows.
Invented the confocal scanning microscope, an optical instrument with unprecedented resolution, while a Junior Fellow at Harvard.
Joined the MIT faculty in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science.
Co-founded the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory with John McCarthy.
Received the ACM Turing Award and published Perceptrons with Seymour Papert, a influential and controversial book on neural network limitations.
Published The Society of Mind, a seminal work proposing that intelligence emerges from many simple agents.
Died on January 24, 2016, in Boston, Massachusetts.

name: John McCarthy
milestone_by_age_26: Coined 'artificial intelligence' in 1955 at age 28 and invented Lisp in 1958; by 26 had a PhD in mathematics from Princeton but no distinctive personal milestone in computing.
early_history_summary: Born in Boston to an Irish immigrant father and Lithuanian immigrant mother, McCarthy was a precocious student who taught himself calculus from Caltech textbooks in high school and graduated early. He earned a BS from Caltech (1948) and a PhD from Princeton (1951) in mathematics, then stayed on as an instructor. His interest in machine intelligence began at Caltech and Princeton, but his seminal AI contributions came after age 26.
family_context_summary: Father was an Irish immigrant and member of the Communist Party; mother was a Lithuanian immigrant. Family relocated frequently during the Great Depression. Father was involved in the Amalgamated Clothing Workers union.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. Parents were working-class immigrants; no evidence of technical or scientific domain expertise in the family.
evidence_summary: McCarthy was the son of working-class immigrants and showed early mathematical precocity, teaching himself calculus and graduating high school two years early. He earned his PhD from Princeton at 24, which is notable but not a distinctive personal milestone. His seminal contributions — coining 'artificial intelligence,' the Dartmouth workshop, and inventing Lisp — came at ages 28-31, just beyond the age-26 cutoff.

name: Norbert Wiener
milestone_by_age_26: Earned a PhD from Harvard at age 18 in 1913 with a dissertation on mathematical logic, then studied under Bertrand Russell at Cambridge and David Hilbert at Göttingen.
early_history_summary: Wiener was a child prodigy homeschooled intensively by his father Leo, a Harvard professor of Slavic languages, who personally tutored him in mathematics using demanding and sometimes harsh methods. He graduated high school at 11, earned a BA from Tufts at 14, and a PhD from Harvard at 18, then studied under Russell and Hilbert in Europe before joining MIT in 1919.
family_context_summary: Son of Leo Wiener, a Harvard professor of Slavic languages, and Bertha Kahn, daughter of a department store owner. Father personally directed Norbert's intensive education from early childhood, tutoring him in mathematics with demanding and sometimes harsh methods.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father Leo Wiener was a Harvard professor with deep mathematical interests who personally and intensively tutored Norbert in mathematics from childhood. Leo was related to mathematician Leon Lichtenstein. This father-directed homeschooling was the primary engine of Wiener's extraordinary early development.
primary_early_advantage_tags: father-tutored mathematics, child prodigy, Harvard professor family, intensive homeschooling, Russell and Hilbert
evidence_summary: Wiener was a legendary child prodigy whose father Leo, a Harvard professor, personally directed his intensive mathematical education from early childhood using demanding methods. He graduated high school at 11, earned a BA from Tufts at 14, and a PhD from Harvard at 18 in mathematical logic. He then studied under Bertrand Russell at Cambridge and David Hilbert at Göttingen, placing him at the centers of early 20th-century mathematics. The father-driven homeschooling was the dominant early advantage, creating an extreme case of family-domain apprenticeship. He joined MIT in 1919 and later founded cybernetics.
starting_point: Born in Columbia, Missouri to Leo Wiener, a Harvard professor of Slavic languages, and Bertha Kahn, daughter of a department store owner; father personally directed his intensive early education in mathematics and languages.
current_position: Died March 18, 1964 at age 69 in Stockholm, Sweden while on a lecture tour; final role: Institute Professor Emeritus of Mathematics at MIT.

trajectory.event: Earned a PhD from Harvard in mathematical logic at age 18 and published his first mathematical paper in the Messenger of Mathematics.
Studied under Bertrand Russell at Cambridge University and David Hilbert at the University of Göttingen, the two leading centers of mathematics in Europe.
Appointed as an instructor in mathematics at MIT, beginning a 45-year association with the institution.
Received the Bôcher Memorial Prize from the American Mathematical Society for his work in mathematical analysis.
Published Cybernetics: Or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine, founding the field of cybernetics.
Awarded the National Medal of Science for his contributions to mathematics, engineering, and biological sciences.
Died on March 18, 1964, in Stockholm, Sweden, while on a lecture tour.

name: Konrad Zuse
milestone_by_age_26: Z1 computer completed in 1938 at age 28 and Z3 in 1941 at age 31; by 26 had graduated in civil engineering and just started building the Z1 but had not completed a functional machine.
early_history_summary: Born in Berlin, Zuse moved to East Prussia as a child where his father was a postal clerk. He studied civil engineering at Technische Hochschule Berlin, graduating in 1935. After working briefly at Henschel Aircraft Company on stress analysis, he resigned to become an inventor and began building the Z1 computer in his parents' apartment in 1936, completing it in 1938.
family_context_summary: Born in Berlin; father was a postal clerk. Family moved to East Prussia when Zuse was young. Not documented in reviewed sources beyond this.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. Father was a postal clerk, not in a technical or engineering field.
evidence_summary: Zuse was the son of a postal clerk in Germany and studied civil engineering, graduating in 1935. He began building the Z1, the first programmable binary computing machine, in 1936 in his parents' apartment, but it was not completed until 1938 when he was 28. His most significant achievement, the fully functional Z3, came in 1941 at age 31. By 26 he had only started construction and had no completed milestone.
